segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Director Ang Lee said his intention with Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon was simply to make the best martial arts film possible. The artistic success and popularity of the result suggest that he succeeded. Working from a screenplay by his longtime collaborator James Schamus (b. 1959), Lee assembled a cast of Asian action superstars who also had the artistic talent needed to let the story flow.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Lee also made a brilliant decision in recruiting the famous fight choreographer Yuen Woo-ping. Inspired by the physicality of Chinese theater, Yuen defies the laws of physics, hoisting the actors on wires so they can fight atop the trees, skim across water like skipping stones, run up walls and, several times, battle in midair. For Western audiences, perhaps unaccustomed to these aerial ballets, the sight of the opening scene's chase on foot across village rooftops on a moonlit night proved immediately and irresistibly appealing.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Chow Yun-Fat (b. 1955), Michelle Yeoh (b. 1962) and the relative newcomer Zhang Ziyi (b. 1979) handle the supernatural physical demands of their roles with ease, but their performances never fall short of the impressive action scenes. Indeed, one of the reasons Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon became such a sensation was the attention the film paid to plot and character development, two rarities even for the most ambitious martial arts films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A strongly feminist undercurrent also runs through Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, adding another layer of intelligence. The female characters fight for different reasons, but most of them seem to be fighting for respect in a man's world. Having run away from home, young Zhang, passing herself off as a male warrior, is attacked at an inn by several truculent fighters. Lee turns the inevitable beating she gives dozens of would-be attackers into a joke, a hyperkinetic variation on the old bar brawl. But part of Zhang's passionate response seems to stem from a long-held resentment at believing she would be scorned rather than respected (or feared) as a formidable opponent if they knew she was a woman.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Lee modulates every scene of the film with similar nuance and sensitivity. His fight sequences play out as much as psychological contests as sword fights, with clashes between innocence and experience, peace and rage. Still, Lee leaves room for lightness and visual poetry, striking a rare balance of excitement, beauty, humor and intelligence.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Chinese director with the greatest international impact was Taiwan's Ang Lee (b. 1954), whose first two films, Tui shou (Pushing Hands, 1992) and Xi yan (The Wedding Banquet, 1993), are set in the United States and depict the culture clash between Asia and the West. While other Taiwanese directors such as Edward Yang (1947-2007) made art films, like Yi yi (2000), Lee directed the stylish martial arts film Wo Hu Cang Long (Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, 2000), which inspired Ying Xiong (Hero, 2002) and Shi Mian Mai Fu (House of Flying Daggers, 2004).

segments.original: These visually splendid epics found eager audiences abroad and sealed the internationalization of East Asian cinema. This can also be seen in the work of Hong Kong director Wong Kar-Wai (b. 1956), who in films such as Hua Yang De Nian Hua (In the Mood for Love, 2000) opted for a so-called "MTV aesthetic," discarding the austerity of Asian art cinema in favor of the style of international commercials and music videos.

segments.original: While Chinese directors were still wrestling with censorship, South Korean cinema benefited from its liberation from state control in the democratic era. The result was the maturing of the country's filmmaking, which also began to attract international attention. Hong Sang-Soo (b. 1960) was acclaimed by local and foreign critics for his debut film, Daijiga umule pajinnal (The Day a Pig Fell Into the Well, 1996), which tells four loosely interconnected life stories in modern Seoul.

tracks.title: Learn more: The Ultimate Revenge Story

segments.original: Learn more: The Ultimate Revenge Story.
segments.text: Learn more: The Ultimate Revenge Story.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Mysticism, poetry, school days and a futuristic bedroom are some of the surprises found in Oldboy, a thriller that draws on Oedipal taboos and the blindness of chance, on hypnotism and fate. Part action film, part drama, part psychological thriller, this groundbreaking work introduced South Korean cinema to more viewers than any other. The story is more direct and engaging than that of director Park Chan-Wook's previous film, the popular Boksuneun Naui Geot (Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance, 2002), and it starts explosively. A man is imprisoned for 15 years without any explanation. When he escapes, he has only five days to find those responsible for his incarceration.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: This violent, elegiac masterpiece is based on a Japanese manga by Garon Tsuchiya. Actor Choi Min-sik (b. 1962), who did without stunt doubles, trained rigorously for the role of the hapless victim of a mysterious kidnapping. Dae-su manages to escape from his windowless prison and, once free, in the manner of the Count of Monte Cristo, he swears revenge on the jailer who robbed him of his daughter, his wife and his entire life. Transformed into a ragged fighting machine, like a Korean Charles Bronson in a cheap wig, Dae-su befriends a beautiful sushi-bar chef (Hye-Jeong Kang), whose interest he piques by eating a live squid and then passing out face-first on the counter. That is the blockbuster style of Oldboy. But this complex tale is imbued with a clearly unfolding logic, easily incorporating the film's many flashbacks. The pace of the action is breathtaking, but there is also time for thought. The choreographed fights are both innovative and surprising, and all the violence serves the plot.
